title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service automatically recorded workplace video meetings and shared the audio with the company to train its AI systems, according to a federal lawsuit filed in California. The software joined meetings by default when linked to workplace calendars and recorded without explicit consent from meeting participants, the suit alleges. Users reported discovering these recordings had occurred without their knowledge.

The system was deployed with insufficient consent mechanisms. Otter's privacy policy included a checkbox users could grant permission through, but the lawsuit contends users were misled about what they were authorizing and that many did not understand their conversations would be recorded and shared. The company states it removes identifying information before using recordings for training, but the lawsuit questions the effectiveness of this anonymization. What would have caught this: clearer disclosure of the automatic recording behavior before the software accessed meetings, or requiring explicit opt-in consent from all meeting participants rather than relying on a single user's checkbox.

Whether Otter's practices actually violated users' privacy rights under state and federal law, and whether the company's anonymization process was adequate, are not established by the lawsuit itself. A court has allowed the case to proceed as a class action, but this is not a finding of wrongdoing.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit claims that Otter's software, which transcribes Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams meetings, automatically records sessions by default and shares the audio with the company to improve its artificial intelligence systems. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was violated when he discovered Otter was secretly recording a confidential conversation. The lawsuit contends this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and seeks to represent other California users whose conversations were shared without their knowledge.

The case highlights growing privacy concerns as Otter's service has expanded to about 25 million users worldwide, who have processed over one billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016. Users have reported on social media that the software joins meetings automatically when linked to workplace calendars and records without consent from participants. Otter's privacy policy states it receives permission through a checkbox to train its systems, but the lawsuit argues many users are misled about this practice. The company claims it removes identifying information before using recordings for training, though the lawsuit questions whether this process is effective and transparent.
